body.text: In Rahat, the largest Bedouin city in Israel’s southern Negev desert, a 56-year-old Palestinian woman walked into a polling station on October 27 and voted in an Israeli parliamentary election for the first time. Dressed in black, with only her eyes visible, she declined to give her name or be photographed. But she captured the anger sweeping through Palestinian communities. “The government’s behaviour had hurt our souls,” she said.

Her family lived in an unrecognised Bedouin village without electricity or running water. Building even a modest shelter could invite demolition. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir wanted to demolish everything.

Across the Negev, women who had rarely participated in national elections joined queues outside polling stations. Images and accounts of Bedouin voters arriving on camels, horses, and donkeys circulated during the election. For communities living in remote desert settlements, voting could itself require a considerable journey.

In some Palestinian localities, voters also complained of intimidation, police intervention, and delays at polling stations. The legal rights organisation Adalah reported unusually slow identity checks and questioning of voters. Nimr Abu Shiban, a resident of Rahat, told The Times of Israel that his wife and daughters would not ordinarily have voted. “But the country is in such bad hands that everyone is voting today,” he said.

The turnout drew a reaction from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In most democracies, a political leader would welcome the participation of a previously disengaged section of the electorate. Netanyahu treated the mobilisation of Palestinian citizens, who constitute roughly one-fifth of Israel’s population, as an emergency. He urged Jewish supporters to rush to polling stations. Images of Bedouin voters were used to warn that Palestinian participation threatened the Right.

The underlying message was difficult to miss. The Prime Minister was alarmed that a substantial section of the population was exercising its democratic rights. By Wednesday, October 28, that mobilisation had transformed Israel’s political arithmetic. With 85.6 per cent of the ballots counted, Netanyahu’s alliance was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, Israel’s parliament. The Jewish-led opposition, headed by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, stood at 48. Two Palestinian-led electoral formations, the secular nationalist Joint List and Islamist Ra’am, were projected to secure a combined 19 seats.

Parties opposed to Netanyahu could collectively command 67 seats, comfortably above the 61 required for a parliamentary majority. Yet several of the Jewish-led opposition parties remained unwilling to treat Palestinian lawmakers as acceptable governing partners. Israel had produced an election in which the people who helped deny Netanyahu a majority were also the people his principal challengers hesitated to embrace.
Netanyahu lost but was not defeated

The Israeli journalist Meron Rapoport summed up the electoral verdict: Netanyahu had lost, but he had not been defeated. Although Netanyahu’s coalition had lost about 11 seats compared with the 2022 election, his opponents had failed to secure a governing majority without Palestinian support.

Netanyahu could claim that his message of continued military confrontation and national emergency had retained substantial backing among Jewish voters. Rapoport argued that Netanyahu had persuaded many voters to accept his account of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack. In that account, the Prime Minister shifted responsibility for the security failure towards the military leadership while presenting himself as the leader who subsequently restored Israel’s security. “He will feel that what he proposed to the Jewish voters - to continue the wars, to maintain the state of emergency - has been accepted,” Rapoport wrote in Middle East Eye.

But the more consequential development is the emergence of Palestinian citizens as an indispensable electoral constituency. “The Jewish secular liberal camp has two choices: live forever under Netanyahu… or come to an understanding with the Arab parties and voters,” he added.

For years, Israel’s Jewish opposition parties had calculated that they could defeat Netanyahu without depending on Palestinian votes. They believed a combination of military credentials, nationalist appeals, and opposition to ultra-Orthodox political influence would be sufficient.

The election demonstrated the limits of that strategy. Rapoport argued that without the extraordinary Palestinian turnout, Netanyahu’s coalition might have secured a majority with relative ease. This was a moment of political agency for Palestinian citizens who had long been excluded from the country’s governing arrangements. But it also carried a warning. The Israeli Right might respond to the unexpected electoral strength of Palestinian citizens by seeking ways to prevent them from exercising such influence again.
Unwanted kingmakers

The overall turnout reached 77.7 per cent, the highest since 1999. Channel 12 estimated Palestinian participation at around 80 per cent, although the election authorities had not released an official demographic breakdown.

For decades, many Palestinians holding Israeli citizenship had debated whether voting in the Knesset legitimised a state that constitutionally privileges Jewish national identity. Some boycotted elections on principle. Others considered participation necessary to defend their communities against increasingly hostile governments. This time, many appeared to conclude that abstention would only strengthen Netanyahu’s coalition with Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

Sami Abou Shahadeh, a prominent Arab-Israeli politician associated with the Balad party, told Frontline that the election had exposed the contradiction at the heart of Israeli democracy. His party is part of the Joint List. “If we lived in a normal, democratic, non-racist country, Netanyahu would have lost the election,” he said. He argued that Netanyahu’s parliamentary camp had lost its majority, while parties opposing his continued rule collectively held enough seats to form a government. “In reality, Netanyahu’s camp did lose the election, dropping from 68 seats to 54, and the contest should have ended there,” he said, referring to an earlier projection. “But because of the racism within Israeli society, we are still debating whether or not this was a decisive outcome.”

Abou Shahadeh’s criticism went beyond Netanyahu. He questioned why Palestinian lawmakers were excluded from calculations of a legitimate parliamentary majority when they had been elected through the same process as Jewish legislators. “Eisenkot has a majority to form a government, yet what prevents him from doing so is his own racism,” he said. He also pointed to Eisenkot’s Moroccan Jewish ancestry. “Eisenkot, a leader of Arab, specifically Moroccan, descent, says he refuses to sit with Arabs. This is a racist society.”

His remarks reflected a larger frustration. Palestinian citizens were being encouraged to participate in elections, but their elected representatives were still considered politically unacceptable by much of the Jewish establishment.
Joint List, Balad and Ra’am

For readers unfamiliar with Israeli politics, the names of the Palestinian electoral formations can be confusing. The Joint List is an electoral alliance rather than a single party. In this election, it brought together three distinct political organisations: Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad.

Hadash is a left-wing formation rooted in communist and socialist politics. It includes Jewish and Palestinian members and emphasises equality, workers’ rights, and opposition to occupation. Ta’al, associated with veteran parliamentarian Ahmad Tibi, concentrates on the political and civil rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Balad, with which Abou Shahadeh is associated, takes a more explicitly Palestinian nationalist position. It advocates transforming Israel into a state of equal citizenship rather than one that gives constitutional preference to Jewish national identity. Balad also stresses Palestinian collective rights and has historically resisted participation in Zionist-led governments. The Joint List was projected to win 12 seats.

The second formation is Ra’am, the Hebrew acronym for the United Arab List, headed by Mansour Abbas. Ra’am emerged from the southern branch of Israel’s Islamic Movement. It combines socially conservative roots with a pragmatic approach to parliamentary politics.

Abbas argues that Palestinian citizens cannot wait indefinitely for a comprehensive peace settlement before demanding improvements in schools, housing, municipal budgets, and public security. In 2021, Ra’am became the first independent Arab-majority party to join an Israeli governing coalition, entering the administration led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. In 2026, Abbas took the party further towards a civic political identity by separating its decision-making from the Islamic Movement’s Shura Council.

Ra’am was projected to win seven seats, compared with five in the outgoing Knesset. According to its approved candidate list, the seven prospective lawmakers are Mansour Abbas, Yoav Segalovitz, Waleed Taha, Waleed Al-Hawashla, Iman Khatib-Yassin, Dr Yasser Hujeirat, and Ibrahim Al-Turi.

The second name is the most unusual. Yoav Segalovitz is a Jewish Zionist, a former senior police officer, a former member of the centrist Yesh Atid party, and a former Deputy Public Security Minister. His inclusion near the top of an Arab-majority party’s electoral list is politically significant. Abbas has sought to demonstrate that Ra’am can attract Jewish politicians willing to cooperate on questions of civil equality and public safety. It also exposes an irony in Israeli politics. A Palestinian-led Islamist party is prepared to elect a Jewish Zionist to parliament, while several Jewish-led parties refuse to enter government with elected Palestinian representatives.

The Joint List has taken a different position. Its leaders have offered to support an alternative government from outside the coalition, without necessarily accepting ministerial office. Abbas has argued that Palestinian citizens must work with the Israeli establishment to secure tangible improvements. The Joint List, by contrast, has insisted that Palestinian citizens cannot separate their struggle for equality inside Israel from the fate of Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank, and the diaspora.

Yousef Jabareen, chairman of the Joint List, has identified four conditions for supporting a government that replaces Netanyahu: action against organised crime, development and expansion of Palestinian communities, equal civil rights, and a clear political process towards an independent Palestinian state. The final demand links the immediate concerns of Palestinian citizens inside Israel to the unresolved question of Palestinian self-determination.
For Eisenkot and his prospective allies, it presents a difficult choice.
The grievances behind the vote

The anger driving Palestinian participation was not confined to the war in Gaza. Across Galilee, from Nazareth and Sakhnin to Tamra and Shefa-Amr, Palestinian citizens confront inequalities often obscured by Israel’s image as a prosperous high-tech economy. Beside affluent Jewish neighbourhoods, nearby Arab localities struggle with inadequate infrastructure, overcrowded housing, and limited municipal resources.

According to the Israel Democracy Institute’s 2024 statistical report, 95 per cent of Arab localities fell within the four lowest categories of Israel’s 10-category socioeconomic ranking. In 2023, 38.4 per cent of Arab families lived below the poverty line.
Organised crime has compounded these inequalities. The Abraham Initiatives recorded 252 Arab citizens killed in circumstances related to crime and violence during 2025.

The political commentator Tal Schneider said the gap between Jewish society and Arab society is just horrible. She rejected the suggestion that the violence reflected some inherent characteristic of Arab society, pointing instead to weak policing, poverty, and years of inadequate investment.
Israel’s caste-like divide

The election also revealed another, less visible division within Jewish Israeli society. Although all Jewish citizens belong to the country’s politically dominant national community, they do not share a uniform social or historical background.

Israel’s Jewish population is broadly divided between Ashkenazi Jews, whose family origins lie in Europe, and Mizrahi Jews, whose roots are in the Middle East and North Africa. The categories overlap in some families and do not determine individual political views, but they have played an important role in Israeli politics.

For decades after Israel’s establishment in 1948, Ashkenazi Jews dominated the country’s political, military, academic, and economic institutions. Many Mizrahi immigrants, arriving from Morocco, Iraq, Yemen, and other countries, encountered poorer housing, limited opportunities, and discrimination.

The resulting resentments helped reshape Israeli politics. The Labour establishment, historically dominated by Ashkenazi elites, lost its monopoly over political power when Menachem Begin’s Likud won the 1977 election.

Likud subsequently developed a durable base among Mizrahi and working-class voters. This produced a political paradox that remains visible today. Netanyahu himself comes from an Ashkenazi family, as have many prominent Likud leaders. Yet the party’s strongest and most loyal constituencies include substantial numbers of Mizrahi voters.

His principal challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, belongs to a Moroccan Jewish family. Yet his Yashar party draws support from constituencies associated with Israel’s more secular, liberal, and economically established centre, including many Ashkenazi voters.

An Ashkenazi-led Likud continues to draw strength from Mizrahi resentment towards old elites, while a Mizrahi challenger seeks to replace Netanyahu with support from voters historically associated with those elites. Were Eisenkot to become Prime Minister, he would be the first Israeli leader of Mizrahi family origin to hold the office.

There is another dimension to the anti-Netanyahu vote. The proposition that removing Netanyahu could restore Israel’s international standing has become part of the political debate. For sections of European Jews, replacing Netanyahu is associated with repairing relations with Western governments and societies.
Can Eisenkot cross the divide?

Eisenkot represents an alternative to Netanyahu’s leadership rather than a fundamental rejection of Israel’s prevailing security doctrine. A former military chief, he has opposed Palestinian statehood in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack. His prospective coalition partners include politicians whose positions on Palestinian rights are often as restrictive as those of Netanyahu’s existing allies.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett supports Israeli sovereignty over substantial areas of the occupied West Bank. Avigdor Liberman, a former Defence Minister, has long advocated hard-line security policies. Both previously served under Netanyahu. Both now oppose his continued leadership. Their political differences with him are real, but they should not be mistaken for agreement with Palestinian demands for sovereignty and self-determination.

Eisenkot has set conditions for cooperation with Arab parties, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, acceptance of national service obligations, and unequivocal condemnation of Hamas. His right-wing allies have been even more categorical in rejecting cooperation. Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, has taken a different position. “We have a majority. We have responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens,” he declared.
What happens next

President Isaac Herzog will consult parliamentary parties before selecting the lawmaker he believes has the strongest prospect of forming a government. The candidate will ordinarily receive 28 days to assemble a coalition, with a possible extension of 14 days. Further attempts may follow if the first candidate fails.

During that period, Netanyahu remains caretaker Prime Minister. Four principal scenarios now confront Israel. The first is an Eisenkot-led government supported by Palestinian parties. Ra’am has signalled willingness to participate directly, while the Joint List has offered outside parliamentary support.

Israel’s parliamentary rules permit a minority government to take office if it wins a confidence vote, even without 61 affirmative votes. The precedent dates to Yitzhak Rabin’s government in the 1990s, which relied on outside Arab-party support after losing coalition partners.

Such an arrangement would require difficult compromises. The Arab parties would demand action on discrimination, public safety, budgets, and housing. The Joint List would also seek a political process towards Palestinian statehood, a demand likely to encounter resistance from Eisenkot’s right-wing allies.

The second possibility is a national unity government. Herzog has urged political flexibility to avoid another election. A Netanyahu-Eisenkot arrangement could be presented as a response to national security pressures, particularly renewed confrontation with Iran. US interest in Israeli political stability could add momentum to such discussions. Bennett and Liberman, despite opposing Netanyahu, also belong to the Right and have previously worked with him.

Yet Eisenkot has explicitly rejected governing alongside Netanyahu. He would also remember Benny Gantz’s unsuccessful rotation arrangement with Netanyahu in 2020, which collapsed before Gantz could assume the premiership.

Observers say even a unity government could represent a limited achievement for Palestinian voters if it excluded Ben-Gvir and Smotrich. Many Palestinian citizens turned out primarily to remove these two politicians from positions of power.

The third possibility is a realignment within the Right. Individual lawmakers or factions could support a different coalition, although Israel’s anti-defection legislation imposes significant restrictions on politicians who abandon their parliamentary parties. Liberman has suggested that Likud lawmakers might eventually break with Netanyahu. But there is no established evidence that a sufficient number are prepared to do so.

The fourth possibility is another election. Israel endured repeated elections between 2019 and 2022 because competing parties could not assemble stable governments. A fresh vote would prolong Netanyahu’s caretaker premiership and expose all parties to an uncertain electorate. It could also frustrate Palestinian citizens who mobilised in exceptional numbers only to see their parliamentary strength left unused.
An additional uncertainty hangs over coalition negotiations: the possibility of renewed military confrontation with Iran.
Impact on Gaza and the West Bank

For Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, the election raises a more disturbing possibility than the continuation of Netanyahu’s rule. Some observers fear that Netanyahu’s removal could weaken the international pressure currently being exerted on Israel, even if the policies responsible for Palestinian suffering remain substantially unchanged.

A government headed by Eisenkot could present itself as a responsible alternative, promising to repair relations with Western governments, restore institutional discipline, and moderate some of the rhetoric associated with Netanyahu’s far-right ministers.

Such a change could be welcomed by European governments eager to restore diplomatic normality with Israel. The Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem argues that international pressure must not depend on which politician occupies the Prime Minister’s office. B’Tselem representatives Yuli Novak and Yair Dvir warned against treating Netanyahu as the sole architect of Palestinian dispossession. “We are not seeing any possibility of change that will come from within the system,” Dvir said.

Novak, the organisation’s executive director, placed the present crisis within a much longer history. “Settlement, ethnic cleansing, dehumanization, military control, apartheid, these are all things that were there way, way before,” she said. She argued that Netanyahu’s departure would not automatically dismantle the institutions and policies through which Israel exercises control over Palestinian lives.

Jewish settlers living in the occupied West Bank can vote for Israel’s parliament. Palestinians living nearby, subject to Israeli military authority, generally cannot. Palestinians in Gaza also have no vote in Israeli parliamentary elections, despite the profound influence of Israeli military and political decisions over their lives.

Most Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem possess residency rather than Israeli citizenship and likewise cannot participate in national elections. The result is a political system in which millions of people live under varying degrees of Israeli control without enjoying an equal right to determine the government responsible for major decisions affecting their lives.

The election has changed the arithmetic of Israeli politics. Whether it changes the lives of Palestinians will depend not only on who governs Israel, but also on whether the world continues to demand accountability, whichever government takes office.
Iftikhar Gilani is an Indian journalist based in Ankara.
